summary.text: 休 is a compound commonly explained as a person resting by a tree. That picture fits the familiar sense “rest,” but a competing account reads the right-hand shape as marker posts and connects the graph with commendation; the original motivation is unsettled.

formation.text: The main analysis is a semantic compound (會意): 人, a person, together with 木, a tree, pictures a person leaning against the trunk or resting in its shade. Some early tree forms reportedly lean toward the person to suggest shelter, while remaining 木 rather than 禾. A competing proposal interprets the right side as 禾-shaped military marker posts and the graph as recognition of merit, so the person-and-tree reading is not certain.

components.text: 人 is the person in the person-and-tree analysis; its profile is described as turned toward or leaning against the tree. Here it contributes a depicted person to the scene.

木 represents the tree in the common analysis. Some early forms reportedly bend its top toward the person to suggest shade; the account identifies it as 木, despite resemblance to 禾. The competing marker-post interpretation disputes this identification.

history.text: Catalog records list 休 in oracle-bone and bronze examples and in the seal-script category. The catalog’s graph reading identifies a person and 木, but the inscription dates, readings, and contexts were not independently checked here; no surviving sequence of graphic changes is established by this evidence.

The transmitted Shuowen explanation defines 休 as “cease/rest” and analyzes it as a person relying on a tree. This is an old lexicographic interpretation, not independent proof of the graph’s original motivation. A competing account proposes a 禾-like element depicting paired military gate markers and a meaning related to commendation; the available accounts do not resolve the disagreement.
No early glyph image in this dossier was verified as a direct view of an ancient artifact. The bronze-style image located in research is a modern redraw, so it cannot settle the competing analyses.

uncertainties.text: The person-by-a-tree interpretation is widely represented in the dossier, but the marker-post explanation materially disputes both the right-hand element and the graph’s original motivation. The evidence does not settle which account is correct.
Reported bronze and received-text examples show several uses, but their dates and contexts were not independently verified. The earliest lexical sense cannot be securely ranked from this evidence.

senses.text: Rest is supported by received-text examples and by the transmitted Shuowen definition; the evidence here does not establish it as the earliest attested sense.
The graph is historically used with the sense “stop” or “cease”; the cited examples do not establish when this use arose relative to “rest.”
A source proposes a link from shade to shelter or protection and cites textual and inscriptional uses, but the evidence does not establish the chronology or each semantic bridge.
Reported inscriptional uses include favor or reward. Their dates and contexts are not independently established here, so their relation to rest or shelter remains uncertain.
A competing graph analysis cites a bronze use glossed “good/commendable” and connects it with recognition of merit; this does not settle the graph’s origin or the chronology of this sense.
The common current meaning includes rest or taking a break.

developments.text: Both rest and stopping are attested, but the available evidence does not show that one meaning developed from the other.
A proposed connection through resting in tree shade links rest with shelter, but the cited material does not establish the direction or chronology of this development.
A source proposes that shelter or protection extended to benefaction or reward; the evidence does not independently establish this semantic bridge or its order.

limitations.text: The dossier does not securely rank the earliest lexical sense or date the cited uses. The source-proposed links among shade, protection, favor, reward, goodness, pleasure, rest, and stopping should not be read as a proven sequence.

overview.text: 休 is commonly read as a person resting beside a tree: its two pictured elements form a scene. A competing explanation interprets the right side as military marker posts, leaving the graph’s original motivation unsettled.

components.text: 人 depicts the person in the common scene, leaning toward the tree.
木 depicts the tree; the marker-post account disputes this identification.

relationships.text: In the common person-and-tree interpretation, 人 depicts the person in the scene represented by 休.
In the common analysis, 木 depicts the tree against which the person leans or beneath which the person rests; this identification is disputed by the marker-post account.
